title: Fuzzy Message Detection
note: Defines FMD: a recipient derives a detection key that flags all true messages plus non-matching ones at a chosen false-positive rate p, so detection can be outsourced to an untrusted server with detection ambiguity. Costs (CCA-secure scheme, p=2^-n up to n=24): 68-byte flag ciphertext, 1.927 ms to create, 0.548 ms to test at p=3%. Fractional-p scheme (garbled circuits): 0.3-1.2 MB ciphertexts, 18.1 ms create, 9.6 ms test. Privacy depends on p: lower p means less bandwidth but a smaller anonymity set.
bitmessage_link: Attacks Bitmessage's flood-and-trial-decrypt directly: the recipient hands a detection key to an untrusted node that filters the board, so the client downloads roughly a fraction p of traffic instead of everything, at the price of an anonymity set of size about p times the traffic.

title: The Effect of False Positives: Why Fuzzy Message Detection Leads to Fuzzy Privacy Guarantees?
note: First formal privacy analysis of FMD: recipient unlinkability, relationship anonymity and temporal detection ambiguity, plus a differential-privacy-style relaxation and simulation on real communication data. Shows the false-positive rate must be set from the traffic graph, not a fixed constant; no new cost numbers, it quantifies how privacy degrades as the detection precision rises.
bitmessage_link: Quantifies how much anonymity a Bitmessage-style recipient keeps when it downloads only a filtered subset of traffic; shows fuzzy filtering leaks relationship and timing information over repeated rounds.

title: Private Signaling
note: Defines private signaling in the UC framework: sender posts a message and a signal; only the recipient learns the location, with constant work for sender and recipient. Two server-aided protocols: one TEE server (about 116-157 ms per signal in the paper's setting, M=100 recipients), one two-server garbled-circuit protocol (minutes per signal). Full recipient privacy, unlike FMD, at the price of per-signal server work that grows with recipients.
bitmessage_link: Same board-plus-signal model as Bitmessage's flooded object pool, with an outsourced detection step so recipients no longer scan everything; trust moves to a TEE or to non-colluding servers.

title: Scalable Private Signaling
note: TEE plus ORAM private signaling that hides the recipient even while it fetches signals. Server with 1 million recipients and 10 million messages: under 70 ms per sent message, under 6 s to serve a retrieval request for 100 signals. Orders of magnitude faster than prior signaling and OMR but rests on a trusted hardware assumption.
bitmessage_link: Same board-plus-signal model as Bitmessage's flooded object pool, with an outsourced detection step so recipients no longer scan everything; trust moves to a TEE or to non-colluding servers.

title: Private Signaling Secure Against Actively Corrupted Servers
note: TEE-free private signaling with two non-colluding servers, either of which may be actively corrupted; retrieval is cast as a PSI-like problem with custom ZK proofs for consistency with the board. Digest 33.57 KB for a board of 2^19 messages; retrieving signals takes about 2 minutes on 16 threads over a LAN.
bitmessage_link: Same board-plus-signal model as Bitmessage's flooded object pool, with an outsourced detection step so recipients no longer scan everything; trust moves to a TEE or to non-colluding servers.

title: Multi-server Fuzzy Message Detection
note: Extends FMD to several servers holding different detection keys extracted from one secret key, so the receiver combines their results locally: servers can use high false-positive rates (more privacy) while the combined rate seen by the receiver stays low (less bandwidth). Formalises stealth public keys for FMD and gives two constructions, one with short public keys. No benchmark numbers in the abstract.
bitmessage_link: Attacks Bitmessage's flood-and-trial-decrypt directly: the recipient hands a detection key to an untrusted node that filters the board, so the client downloads roughly a fraction p of traffic instead of everything, at the price of an anonymity set of size about p times the traffic.

title: Post Quantum Fuzzy Stealth Signatures and Applications
note: Combines stealth signatures with FMD in a lattice-based, post-quantum scheme resistant to unbounded key exposure; the fuzzy tag lets a payee outsource scanning of one-time public keys. Compact fuzzy tag and stealth signature, built to be implementable by current cryptocurrencies; see paper Table 1 for size comparison with pairing and lattice-delegation stealth signatures.
bitmessage_link: A post-quantum route for recipients to find one-time keys without scanning all outputs; the stealth-key part replaces Bitmessage's reuse of a static address key.

title: Oblivious Signaling
note: Asks whether a single untrusted server can support asynchronous delivery without learning destinations and without paying FHE scan cost on every retrieval. Argues OMR makes the retrieval of the whole board the central operation and pays heavy homomorphic work each time; proposes oblivious signaling as a cheaper structure. See the paper for the new construction and costs.
bitmessage_link: Targets the same trade-off as Bitmessage's flood-and-scan model: delivering without per-recipient inboxes (which leak routing) and without every recipient scanning.

title: Oblivious Message Retrieval
note: Introduces OMR: untrusted servers detect all messages for a recipient under FHE and compress them into a compact encrypted digest the recipient decodes, with privacy, soundness and completeness even if all others collude. Digest is a few bits per message scanned; server cost about $1 per million messages scanned; recipient decodes the digest in under about 20 ms. Later work cites about 0.1 s of server time and about 1 KB overhead per message and 132 KB public key for this baseline.
bitmessage_link: Removes the need for every recipient to download and trial-decrypt the whole board, which is Bitmessage's recipient-ambiguity mechanism, while keeping the server blind to who each message is for; stronger than a fuzzy filter but needs FHE or two non-colluding servers.

title: Group Oblivious Message Retrieval
note: Extends OMR to messages with several recipients (group chats, multi-output transactions) by encoding many recipient clues into one polynomial or multilinear function evaluated under FHE; server cost grows slowly with group size and recipient cost is independent of it. Server cost about $3.36 per million messages scanned with up to 15 recipients per message.
bitmessage_link: Removes the need for every recipient to download and trial-decrypt the whole board, which is Bitmessage's recipient-ambiguity mechanism, while keeping the server blind to who each message is for; stronger than a fuzzy filter but needs FHE or two non-colluding servers.

title: PerfOMR: Oblivious Message Retrieval with Reduced Communication and Computation
note: Replaces LWE clue encryption with Ring-LWE. Protocol 1: retrieval circuit evaluated 13.8x faster than prior work. Protocol 2: public key about 235x smaller, message about 1.6x smaller, about 40 ms per message, still more than 2.5x faster than prior OMR (prior: about 0.1 s per message, about 1 KB overhead per message, 132 KB key).
bitmessage_link: Removes the need for every recipient to download and trial-decrypt the whole board, which is Bitmessage's recipient-ambiguity mechanism, while keeping the server blind to who each message is for; stronger than a fuzzy filter but needs FHE or two non-colluding servers.

title: HomeRun: High-efficiency Oblivious Message Retrieval, Unrestricted
note: OMR with two semi-honest non-colluding servers, no cap on pertinent messages (no message-balance exhaustion), unlinkability across repeated requests, and server-side deletion of retrieved messages. Total server runtime 3830x less than the FHE OMR of Liu et al. and at least 1459x less than the two-server design of Madathil et al. (single thread, WAN).
bitmessage_link: Removes the need for every recipient to download and trial-decrypt the whole board, which is Bitmessage's recipient-ambiguity mechanism, while keeping the server blind to who each message is for; stronger than a fuzzy filter but needs FHE or two non-colluding servers.

title: Snake-eye Resistant PKE from LWE for Oblivious Message Retrieval and Robust Encryption
note: Proves a prior OMR (OMRp2) is DoS-resistant under standard LWE and gives DoS-PerfOMR, 12x faster than OMRp2 and close to the fastest non-DoS-resistant OMR (which the paper attacks). Introduces snake-eye resistance (hard to encrypt the same message under two keys) and the LWEmongrass PKE; shows snake-eye resistance implies robust PKE, giving the first lattice robust PKE outside the KEM-DEM paradigm.
bitmessage_link: Addresses the spam problem that Bitmessage handles with per-object proof-of-work: a malicious sender cannot craft clues that overload or mislead the retrieval server.

title: SophOMR: Improved Oblivious Message Retrieval from SIMD-Aware Homomorphic Compression
note: New homomorphic compression using the SIMD structure of the HE scheme. Versus PerfOMR for 65,536 payloads of 612 bytes with up to 50 pertinent: 3.4x lower runtime, 2.2x smaller digest, 1.5x smaller key; the compression step alone is 7.5x faster.
bitmessage_link: Removes the need for every recipient to download and trial-decrypt the whole board, which is Bitmessage's recipient-ambiguity mechanism, while keeping the server blind to who each message is for; stronger than a fuzzy filter but needs FHE or two non-colluding servers.

title: InstantOMR: Oblivious Message Retrieval with Low Latency and Optimal Parallelizability
note: Hybrid of TFHE functional bootstrapping and RLWE operations; messages are processed independently so the detector can stream and answer the moment the recipient comes online. About 860x lower latency than SophOMR and near-optimal scaling with cores.
bitmessage_link: Removes the need for every recipient to download and trial-decrypt the whole board, which is Bitmessage's recipient-ambiguity mechanism, while keeping the server blind to who each message is for; stronger than a fuzzy filter but needs FHE or two non-colluding servers.

title: UnifOMR: Oblivious Message Retrieval with Near-optimal Concrete Efficiency
note: Shows OMR with strong detection-key-unlinkability is at least as hard as PIR (so OMR cannot be much cheaper than PIR), then builds UnifOMR on batch PIR as a black box. 2^19 messages of 612 bytes: about 25 s server time and 4 MB communication, versus over 1250 s and 260 KB for SophOMR (20x-1080x faster); costs are linear-size digests and two rounds.
bitmessage_link: Gives the receiver-privacy cost floor: a Bitmessage-style recipient-hiding retrieval is at best PIR-cost, which bounds what any non-broadcast design can save.

title: Lattice-based Multi-message Multi-recipient KEM/PKE with Malicious Security
note: Attacks existing lattice multi-recipient PKE with maliciously crafted keys (breaks semantic and key privacy) and gives the first lattice mmKEM safe against them; ciphertext for 100 recipients about 8x smaller than naive Kyber. Also improves batched random OT and group OMR.
bitmessage_link: Cuts the per-recipient ciphertext cost of sending one message to many addresses, relevant to chans and group delivery over a shared board.

title: Oblivious Homomorphic Encryption
note: OHE: an FHE service separates the computation spaces of multiple clients while staying blind about whom each result belongs to; used as a generic route to OMR-like services. No benchmark numbers recorded here.
bitmessage_link: Removes the need for every recipient to download and trial-decrypt the whole board, which is Bitmessage's recipient-ambiguity mechanism, while keeping the server blind to who each message is for; stronger than a fuzzy filter but needs FHE or two non-colluding servers.

title: How to Compress Encrypted Data
note: Obliviously compresses n ciphertexts of which at most t decrypt to non-zero into about t ciphertexts, with lower bounds; this is the digest step inside OMR and encrypted search.
bitmessage_link: Supplies the compression step that turns a scan of the whole board into a short digest for the recipient.

title: Oblivious Ciphertext Compression via Linear Codes
note: Deterministic, perfectly correct oblivious compression and decompression of sparse encrypted vectors via linear codes; targets the compression step in OMR, PIR and encrypted search with smaller ciphertexts or lower compute than earlier schemes.
bitmessage_link: Cheaper digest step for the board-scan outsourcing that replaces Bitmessage's trial decryption.

title: Leveraging FPGAs for Homomorphic Matrix-Vector Multiplication in Oblivious Message Retrieval
note: FPGA accelerator for the homomorphic matrix-vector multiplication that dominates OMR detection (high-level synthesis, design-space exploration); 13.86x speedup over the software implementation. Hardware route to lowering the server cost per scanned message.
bitmessage_link: Removes the need for every recipient to download and trial-decrypt the whole board, which is Bitmessage's recipient-ambiguity mechanism, while keeping the server blind to who each message is for; stronger than a fuzzy filter but needs FHE or two non-colluding servers.

title: Effective Anonymous Messaging: the Role of Altruism
note: Empirical game-theory model of FMD on real communication datasets: because each user chooses how much cover traffic to download, selfish users make FMD unviable; the system needs at least a few altruistic users, and betweenness centrality can be used to reach the social optimum.
bitmessage_link: Studies incentives for users to bear cover-traffic cost, the same free-rider issue as Bitmessage's flood.

title: Private Information Retrieval
note: Founding paper. A single database must be downloaded in full (n bits) for perfect privacy; with k>=2 replicated non-colluding servers there are sublinear schemes (two servers: about n^(1/3) communication). The baseline cost every later receiver-privacy scheme is measured against: Bitmessage's flood is the trivial single-server solution.
bitmessage_link: Replaces broadcast-and-trial-decrypt with indexed private retrieval: the recipient fetches only its slots and the server learns nothing about which; works only if the recipient can compute or look up the slot (a rendezvous or mailbox index), which Bitmessage's address-less flooding does not provide.

title: The Capacity of Private Information Retrieval
note: Exact information-theoretic capacity of PIR with N non-communicating databases and K messages: 1 + 1/N + ... + 1/N^(K-1) bits retrieved per bit downloaded. For one database capacity tends to 1/K, i.e. full download; shows what replication buys and fixes the download floor for multi-server PIR mailboxes.
bitmessage_link: Fixes the minimum download for private retrieval from replicated stores, so the saving available over Bitmessage-style full download can be stated exactly.

title: PIR with Compressed Queries and Amortized Query Processing
note: SealPIR: client sends one ciphertext encoding the index and the server obliviously expands it, giving queries 274x smaller and 16.4x cheaper to build than XPIR for 11-24% extra server CPU; adds probabilistic batch codes to amortize multi-query cost. The PIR engine inside Pung.
bitmessage_link: Replaces broadcast-and-trial-decrypt with indexed private retrieval: the recipient fetches only its slots and the server learns nothing about which; works only if the recipient can compute or look up the slot (a rendezvous or mailbox index), which Bitmessage's address-less flooding does not provide.

title: OnionPIR: Response Efficient Single-Server PIR
note: Composes two lattice SHE schemes to cut response size: response overhead 4.2x over the insecure baseline versus about 100x for prior schemes; stateful variant cuts computation 1.8-22x versus stateless.
bitmessage_link: Replaces broadcast-and-trial-decrypt with indexed private retrieval: the recipient fetches only its slots and the server learns nothing about which; works only if the recipient can compute or look up the slot (a rendezvous or mailbox index), which Bitmessage's address-less flooding does not provide.

title: Spiral: Fast, High-Rate Single-Server PIR via FHE Composition
note: Composes Regev and GSW encryption: at least 4.5x smaller queries, 1.5x smaller responses and 2x higher throughput than prior systems; SpiralStreamPack reaches 1.9 GB/s server throughput and rate 0.81 for databases over a million records.
bitmessage_link: Replaces broadcast-and-trial-decrypt with indexed private retrieval: the recipient fetches only its slots and the server learns nothing about which; works only if the recipient can compute or look up the slot (a rendezvous or mailbox index), which Bitmessage's address-less flooding does not provide.

title: One Server for the Price of Two: Simple and Fast Single-Server Private Information Retrieval
note: SimplePIR: under one 32-bit multiply and add per database byte, 10 GB/s/core; for a 1 GB database the client downloads a 121 MB hint then 242 KB per query. DoublePIR: 16 MB hint, 345 KB per query, 7.4 GB/s/core. Applied to private Certificate Transparency auditing: 16 MB download per month plus 150 bytes per TLS connection.
bitmessage_link: Replaces broadcast-and-trial-decrypt with indexed private retrieval: the recipient fetches only its slots and the server learns nothing about which; works only if the recipient can compute or look up the slot (a rendezvous or mailbox index), which Bitmessage's address-less flooding does not provide.

title: FrodoPIR: Simple, Scalable, Single-Server Private Information Retrieval
note: Stateful LWE PIR with a client-independent offline phase: for 1 million 1 KB elements, under 1 s per query, response blow-up under 3.6x, about $1 for 100,000 queries, from a non-optimised Rust implementation.
bitmessage_link: Replaces broadcast-and-trial-decrypt with indexed private retrieval: the recipient fetches only its slots and the server learns nothing about which; works only if the recipient can compute or look up the slot (a rendezvous or mailbox index), which Bitmessage's address-less flooding does not provide.

title: Respire: High-Rate PIR for Databases with Small Records
note: Tuned for small records such as message slots: 6.1 KB online communication to fetch one 256-byte record from over a million records (5.9x less than the best prior lattice scheme); batch queries use 3.4-7.1x less communication at 200-400 MB/s throughput.
bitmessage_link: Small-record PIR matches the message-slot shape of a mailbox board, the regime a Bitmessage replacement would live in.

title: YPIR: High-Throughput Single-Server PIR with Silent Preprocessing
note: No offline hint: for a 32 GB database, 12.1 GB/s/core and 2.5 MB total communication (SimplePIR needs a 724 MB hint plus 1.5 MB). Cuts server cost for private CT auditing by 8x versus the best prior PIR approach.
bitmessage_link: Replaces broadcast-and-trial-decrypt with indexed private retrieval: the recipient fetches only its slots and the server learns nothing about which; works only if the recipient can compute or look up the slot (a rendezvous or mailbox index), which Bitmessage's address-less flooding does not provide.

title: Hintless Single-Server Private Information Retrieval
note: HintlessPIR outsources SimplePIR's hint computation to the server using RLWE with composable preprocessing; 6.37 GB/s on an 8 GB database with no client or server state. TensorPIR lowers communication from square-root to cube-root in the database size.
bitmessage_link: Replaces broadcast-and-trial-decrypt with indexed private retrieval: the recipient fetches only its slots and the server learns nothing about which; works only if the recipient can compute or look up the slot (a rendezvous or mailbox index), which Bitmessage's address-less flooding does not provide.

title: WhisPIR: Stateless Private Information Retrieval with Low Communication
note: Fully stateless PIR for ephemeral clients that appear with only public parameters; needs much less communication than other stateless lattice PIR and is slower only than SimplePIR and HintlessPIR on large entries. Suits frequently updated boards.
bitmessage_link: Replaces broadcast-and-trial-decrypt with indexed private retrieval: the recipient fetches only its slots and the server learns nothing about which; works only if the recipient can compute or look up the slot (a rendezvous or mailbox index), which Bitmessage's address-less flooding does not provide.

title: OnionPIRv2: Efficient Single-Server PIR
note: Engineering update of OnionPIR: 3.7x response overhead for 3 KB entries and up to 1372 MB/s server throughput.
bitmessage_link: Replaces broadcast-and-trial-decrypt with indexed private retrieval: the recipient fetches only its slots and the server learns nothing about which; works only if the recipient can compute or look up the slot (a rendezvous or mailbox index), which Bitmessage's address-less flooding does not provide.

title: InsPIRe: Communication-Efficient PIR with Server-side Preprocessing
note: High throughput and low query size with only server-side preprocessing (no offline download): versus YPIR, 5x smaller keys, up to 50% less online query communication and up to 25% higher throughput.
bitmessage_link: Replaces broadcast-and-trial-decrypt with indexed private retrieval: the recipient fetches only its slots and the server learns nothing about which; works only if the recipient can compute or look up the slot (a rendezvous or mailbox index), which Bitmessage's address-less flooding does not provide.

title: Piano: Extremely Simple, Single-Server PIR with Sublinear Server Computation
note: First practical sublinear-time single-server PIR using only PRFs: amortized O~(sqrt n) server and client time, O(sqrt n) communication per query, sqrt n client storage. For a 100 GB database at 60 ms round trip, 73 ms response time, 40x-900x faster than prior single-server PIR.
bitmessage_link: Sublinear per-message server work is what lets a mailbox server scale to a Bitmessage-sized pool; client keeps O(sqrt n) state.

title: TreePIR: Sublinear-Time and Polylog-Bandwidth Private Information Retrieval from DDH
note: Two-server PIR with sublinear amortized server time and polylogarithmic bandwidth from DDH; outperforms prior two-server schemes in practice.
bitmessage_link: Replaces broadcast-and-trial-decrypt with indexed private retrieval: the recipient fetches only its slots and the server learns nothing about which; works only if the recipient can compute or look up the slot (a rendezvous or mailbox index), which Bitmessage's address-less flooding does not provide.

title: Single Pass Client-Preprocessing Private Information Retrieval
note: Client-preprocessing PIR whose offline phase is exactly one linear pass over the database, concretely optimal for preprocessing; no per-client server storage.
bitmessage_link: Replaces broadcast-and-trial-decrypt with indexed private retrieval: the recipient fetches only its slots and the server learns nothing about which; works only if the recipient can compute or look up the slot (a rendezvous or mailbox index), which Bitmessage's address-less flooding does not provide.

title: Near-Optimal Private Information Retrieval with Preprocessing
note: First single-server PIR with amortized O~(sqrt n) server time and O~(1) bandwidth using client preprocessing and no extra server storage.
bitmessage_link: Replaces broadcast-and-trial-decrypt with indexed private retrieval: the recipient fetches only its slots and the server learns nothing about which; works only if the recipient can compute or look up the slot (a rendezvous or mailbox index), which Bitmessage's address-less flooding does not provide.

title: Limits of Preprocessing for Single-Server PIR
note: Lower bound: with an r-bit public hint and query time t, any computationally secure single-server PIR with preprocessing has t*r = Omega(n log n) for r = Omega(log n) (and t = Omega(n) when r = O(log n)). Bounds how cheap a single-server mailbox can become.
bitmessage_link: Shows per-retrieval server work cannot beat roughly linear unless hint storage grows, limiting any non-broadcast Bitmessage replacement.

title: Doubly Efficient Private Information Retrieval and Fully Homomorphic RAM Computation from Ring LWE
note: Unkeyed doubly efficient PIR from RingLWE: preprocessing O(N^(1+eps)) size and time, then polylog(N) time and communication per query; database updates in time O(N^eps). Theory result, not yet practical.
bitmessage_link: Replaces broadcast-and-trial-decrypt with indexed private retrieval: the recipient fetches only its slots and the server learns nothing about which; works only if the recipient can compute or look up the slot (a rendezvous or mailbox index), which Bitmessage's address-less flooding does not provide.

title: VeriSimplePIR: Verifiability in SimplePIR at No Online Cost for Honest Servers
note: Adds verifiability to SimplePIR so a malicious server cannot equivocate on the database or run selective-failure attacks, at no extra online cost when the server is honest.
bitmessage_link: A message board server that is malicious rather than semi-honest can otherwise tamper per-client; relevant to untrusted mailbox nodes.

title: Communication-Computation Trade-offs in PIR
note: Systematises single-server PIR designs and measures communication versus computation trade-offs across parameter regimes with implementations; a reference for choosing a PIR for a mailbox workload.
bitmessage_link: Replaces broadcast-and-trial-decrypt with indexed private retrieval: the recipient fetches only its slots and the server learns nothing about which; works only if the recipient can compute or look up the slot (a rendezvous or mailbox index), which Bitmessage's address-less flooding does not provide.

title: Private Information Retrieval: A Tutorial and Survey
note: Tutorial and survey: information-theoretic and computational PIR, single and multi-server, with and without preprocessing, plus keyword and batch PIR; compares concrete efficiency of paradigms and gives guidance for choosing one.
bitmessage_link: Replaces broadcast-and-trial-decrypt with indexed private retrieval: the recipient fetches only its slots and the server learns nothing about which; works only if the recipient can compute or look up the slot (a rendezvous or mailbox index), which Bitmessage's address-less flooding does not provide.

title: Call Me By My Name: Simple, Practical Private Information Retrieval for Keyword Queries
note: ChalametPIR: converts any LWE index-PIR into keyword PIR using Binary Fuse filters, with at most 1.08x cost over the index scheme; 6x-11x faster and 3.75x-11.4x cheaper than prior keyword PIR.
bitmessage_link: Keyword PIR lets a recipient look up messages by tag or topic instead of slot number, the case that fits Bitmessage-style tag subscriptions.

title: Practical Keyword Private Information Retrieval from Key-to-Index Mappings
note: Reduces keyword PIR to index PIR through compact key-to-index mappings; 15x-178x less communication and 1.1x-2.4x faster than ChalametPIR; 47 ms for 1 million 32-byte entries.
bitmessage_link: Faster tag lookups for topic-addressed boards.

title: Don't be Dense: Efficient Keyword PIR for Sparse Databases
note: SparsePIR: keyword PIR over sparse key spaces with half the response overhead of prior keyword PIR and no linear-size client mapping; variants trade encoding time and small client state for smaller served databases.
bitmessage_link: Sparse key space is exactly the situation of a tag or topic space far larger than the set of messages present.

title: Key-Privacy in Public-Key Encryption
note: Defines key-privacy (IK-CPA/IK-CCA): an adversary holding a ciphertext cannot tell which of two public keys encrypted it. Shows ElGamal and Cramer-Shoup are key-private, and that RSA-style schemes need care because ciphertexts reveal the modulus. The base property behind every recipient-anonymous broadcast.
bitmessage_link: Bitmessage encrypts every object under the recipient's static public key and relies on every node trial-decrypting; whether ciphertexts leak the recipient key (key-privacy) and whether a wrong key can ever decrypt (robustness) decide if that ambiguity is real.

title: Public Key Encryption with Keyword Search
note: PEKS: a sender appends a searchable tag under the recipient's public key; the recipient hands a trapdoor for a keyword to a gateway that can test tags without reading messages. Built from identity-based encryption; each test is one pairing, so server cost is linear in stored tags. The template for outsourced tag matching (FMD, OMR) and for pub/sub keyword filters.
bitmessage_link: Lets an untrusted server route messages by keyword/recipient tag without reading them, a pre-Bitmessage alternative to trial decryption by every node.

title: Private Searching On Streaming Data
note: A server filters a stream of documents against a hidden keyword criterion using public-key (additively homomorphic) encryption and returns a compact encrypted buffer of matches, without learning the criterion or which documents matched; generalises PIR to a streaming setting and to richer queries. Ancestor of OMR: server work is linear in the stream and the output size is bounded by the expected number of matches.
bitmessage_link: First construction of a server-side private filter over a message stream, the problem Bitmessage solves by every node decrypting everything.

title: Anonymity-preserving Public-Key Encryption: A Constructive Approach
note: Builds a confidential receiver-anonymous channel from a broadcast channel using PKE that is IND-CCA, key-private and weakly robust, and shows weak robustness is necessary while strong robustness is stronger than needed; also proves limitations on what PKE can construct. Formal justification for 'broadcast and let the recipient try all' as an anonymity mechanism.
bitmessage_link: States exactly which encryption properties make Bitmessage's flooded broadcast actually receiver-anonymous: IND-CCA, key-privacy and (weak) robustness of the cipher.

title: Anonymous Broadcast Encryption: Adaptive Security and Efficient Constructions in the Standard Model
note: Defines ANOBE: a multi-recipient ciphertext that does not reveal the recipient set. Generic constructions from key-private IND-CCA PKE and from IBE; introduces anonymous hint systems that speed up decryption so a receiver need not try every ciphertext component. Costs: ciphertext linear in recipients, decryption sped up by hints.
bitmessage_link: Anonymous hint systems are a cryptographic cousin of Bitmessage's tag/trial-decrypt shortcut: a cheap per-component test that avoids a full trial decryption.

title: Anonymous, Robust Post-Quantum Public Key Encryption
note: First systematic study of anonymity (key-privacy) and robustness for PQ PKE: implicit rejection in most PQ KEMs breaks the usual KEM-DEM results, so anonymity/robustness must be re-proved; analyses NIST PQC finalists and alternates.
bitmessage_link: Any post-quantum replacement for Bitmessage's ECIES must keep ciphertexts key-private and robust; this paper says which NIST KEM-based PKEs do.

title: Partitioning Oracle Attacks
note: Shows that AEAD schemes without key commitment let one ciphertext decrypt under many keys, turning a decryption-success oracle into a fast multi-key guessing attack (password guessing in PAKE-like and Shadowsocks settings; speedups in the paper). Relevant to systems that trial-decrypt against many candidate keys.
bitmessage_link: Trial decryption against many candidate keys is the Bitmessage receive path; without key commitment, a crafted object can match many recipients or leak which key matched.

title: Symmetric and Asymmetric Anonymous Authenticated KEM
note: Formal confidentiality, authenticity and anonymity notions for authenticated KEM with optional pre-shared keys, and efficient constructions for each key-combination; anonymity of senders and receivers is the focus.
bitmessage_link: Building block for sender- and recipient-anonymous encrypted objects with authentication, the missing piece in Bitmessage's static-key encryption.

title: Generic Anonymity Wrapper for Messaging Protocols
note: Anonymity Wrapper primitive that wraps ciphertexts of an existing messaging protocol (e.g. Signal) so they look random, with forward anonymity and post-compromise anonymity under state exposure; sender and receiver update algorithms refresh the anonymity state.
bitmessage_link: Gives a way to put receiver anonymity with forward and post-compromise guarantees on top of a ratcheting session, where Bitmessage uses static address keys.

title: Post-Quantum Stealth Address Protocols
note: Three lattice stealth address protocols (LWE, Ring-LWE, Module-LWE); Module-LWE SAP, based on Kyber, outperforms elliptic-curve pairing DKSAP by about 66.8% in scan time of the ephemeral public key registry. Gives the scan-cost metric directly.
bitmessage_link: Bitmessage addresses are static and the public key is looked up by everyone; stealth/one-time addresses give per-message recipient keys, at the cost that the recipient must scan (an ECDH per candidate) unless a tag or detection key short-cuts it.

title: Stealth and Beyond: Attribute-Driven Accountability in Bitcoin Transactions
note: Identity-Based Matchmaking Stealth Signatures: stealth addresses carrying compliance attributes so both sender and recipient satisfy policy, compatible with Bitcoin as is.
bitmessage_link: Shows stealth recipient keys can carry attributes; relevant to proving rights to a recipient tag without revealing the address.

title: Secure Hierarchical Deterministic Wallet Supporting Stealth Address
note: First formal syntax and security model for HD wallets that also support stealth addresses, with a construction secure against derived-key exposure.
bitmessage_link: Bitmessage addresses are static and the public key is looked up by everyone; stealth/one-time addresses give per-message recipient keys, at the cost that the recipient must scan (an ECDH per candidate) unless a tag or detection key short-cuts it.

title: Key-Insulated and Privacy-Preserving Signature Scheme with Publicly Derived Public Key
note: Fixes the master-key-collapse weakness of deterministic wallets and stealth addresses: compromise of one derived key must not expose the master key. Introduces PDPKS with publicly derived public keys and a standard-model/ROM construction.
bitmessage_link: Bitmessage addresses are static and the public key is looked up by everyone; stealth/one-time addresses give per-message recipient keys, at the cost that the recipient must scan (an ECDH per candidate) unless a tag or detection key short-cuts it.

title: Blockchain Stealth Address Schemes
note: Surveys Monero-style dual-key stealth addresses and BIP-32 child-key derivation and proposes an improved scheme with a child number in the address; descriptive rather than a security proof.
bitmessage_link: Bitmessage addresses are static and the public key is looked up by everyone; stealth/one-time addresses give per-message recipient keys, at the cost that the recipient must scan (an ECDH per candidate) unless a tag or detection key short-cuts it.

title: Silent Payments, Formally: Security, Scanning Costs, and Blind Collaborative Payments
note: Game-based unlinkability proofs for BIP-352 and an attack-oriented analysis of receiver scan work: sender-chosen chain data lets an attacker inflate scan cost (quadratic in outputs; the 2026 Kmax cap makes it linear); any compliant scanner needs Omega(N+KM) operations; a set-probing scanner (Specs) is 39x faster on the worst case.
bitmessage_link: Shows a receiver-side scan DoS: whoever can post chain data chooses the receiver's work, the same problem as Bitmessage's flood, bounded there by proof-of-work.

title: BaseSAP: Modular Stealth Address Protocol for Programmable Blockchains
note: Base-layer stealth address protocol for programmable chains with modular cryptographic layers; secp256k1 dual-key instance deployed on Goerli and Sepolia, with gas cost analysis and attack vectors against announcements and registries.
bitmessage_link: Ethereum-style announcement registry is a public board of ephemeral keys scanned by recipients, the same shape as the Bitmessage object pool.

title: Privacy Coins Under Viewing Key Compromise
note: Provable anonymity guarantees for Zcash and Firo when the incoming viewing key is compromised, problems with Monero, and ways a malicious party can surrender all view keys yet evade monitoring. Delegated detection capability has a privacy price.
bitmessage_link: Delegating detection (view or detection keys) is the same trust move FMD and OMR make; this paper measures what an incoming-view-key holder learns.

title: On the Privacy Provisions of Bloom Filters in Lightweight Bitcoin Clients
note: SPV clients upload a Bloom filter of their addresses so full nodes forward only relevant transactions; the paper shows analytically and empirically that a client with a modest number of addresses (under 20) leaks almost all of them, and that restarts or multiple filters make it worse.
bitmessage_link: Empirical proof that tag or Bloom-filter topic subscriptions to an untrusted relay leak the subscriber's interests; applies to any Bitmessage-style stream/tag subscription.

title: CryptoNote v 2.0
note: Defines one-time destination keys: the sender derives a per-output key from the recipient's two-key address and a transaction public key; the recipient finds its outputs by testing every output in every transaction with its view key, one elliptic-curve operation per candidate. Scanning cost is linear in chain outputs.
bitmessage_link: Bitmessage addresses are static and the public key is looked up by everyone; stealth/one-time addresses give per-message recipient keys, at the cost that the recipient must scan (an ECDH per candidate) unless a tag or detection key short-cuts it.

title: Zero to Monero: Second Edition
venue: Monero Research Lab technical guide (v1.0.0 2018; v2.0.0 2020 downloaded)
note: Technical guide to Monero cryptography including one-time addresses, view keys, subaddresses and the wallet's per-output scan; explains why a view key lets a third party identify (not spend) all incoming outputs and why subaddresses raise scan cost.
bitmessage_link: Bitmessage addresses are static and the public key is looked up by everyone; stealth/one-time addresses give per-message recipient keys, at the cost that the recipient must scan (an ECDH per candidate) unless a tag or detection key short-cuts it.

title: Kerblam: Anonymous Messaging System Protecting Both Senders and Recipients
note: Combines OMR (HomeRun) with oblivious shuffling over two non-colluding servers for sender-and-recipient unlinkability without requiring online receivers; an ORAM- variant handles larger messages. For 2^20 messages of 1 KB, 5.577 s to transmit a message.
bitmessage_link: Offline-receiver delivery with both sides hidden, the property Bitmessage gets only by flooding and PoW; here at the cost of two non-colluding servers.

title: Myco: Unlocking Polylogarithmic Accesses in Metadata-Private Messaging
note: Drops PIR (quadratic O(N^2) server computation in users) for an oblivious data structure with an asymmetric two-server write/read split, giving O(N log^2 N) work; throughput up to 302x over multi-server and 2,219x over single-server PIR-based systems.
bitmessage_link: Mailbox/board systems that replace Bitmessage's flood with indexed or oblivious retrieval; they hide the recipient from the storage nodes but need a rendezvous or shared-secret schedule that Bitmessage addresses do not give.

title: Private Identity-based Bulletin Boards for Anonymous Messaging and Other Online Services
note: PIB3: anyone encrypts to an identity and a public epoch; only the key holder can locate, retrieve and decrypt the record. One corrupted non-colluding server learns only the epoch, database size and retrieval count; multi-server extension gives coalition privacy whenever the underlying multi-server PIR does. Needs no pre-exchanged keys, aimed at disrupted and censored networks.
bitmessage_link: Identity-addressed variant of a Bitmessage-like board: the sender needs only the recipient's address string, and the recipient fetches by PIR instead of trial decryption.

title: Verbeth: Secure Messaging with Metadata Minimization over Public Blockchain Logs
note: Private messaging whose transport is a public blockchain log; first contact via long-term KEM with trial decryption, or via a private signaling service on trusted hardware; ongoing conversation uses topic rotation driven by off-chain ratchet state to prevent topic and conversation linkability. Analyses metadata leakage and the economic cost of on-chain messaging.
bitmessage_link: Closest modern analogue of Bitmessage on a public log: trial decryption at first contact, rotating topics afterwards instead of one global flood.

title: AOT: Anonymization by Oblivious Transfer
note: Mixnet whose final delivery uses oblivious transfer: level-3 nodes publish tags on a bulletin board, a receiver spots its tag (derived from a shared secret) and fetches the message by OT, so receiver anonymity survives even if all nodes are covert adversaries; works for offline receivers; receivers send periodic dummy requests. No benchmark numbers in the abstract.
bitmessage_link: OT-based mailbox: the tag on a board plays the part of Bitmessage's decryptable object, but retrieval is oblivious, so a fetching node cannot link receiver to message.

title: AnNotify: A Private Notification Service
note: Private notification of events (new mail, presence) using anonymous channels, sharding, dummy queries and Bloom filters: a subscriber downloads only a shard of the event database; false positives add cover. Scales past the roughly 1 million user limit of DP5 for IT-PIR-based notification and gives a concrete adversary-advantage bound for repeated observation.
bitmessage_link: Topic/shard-based pub/sub notification with Bloom filters: a direct mid-way design between Bitmessage's full flood and per-recipient PIR.

title: Talek: Private Group Messaging with Hidden Access Patterns
note: Group messaging over untrusted servers using information-theoretic PIR; a shared log secret determines a pseudorandom sequence of locations that readers follow without coordination; blocked cuckoo hashing for the IT-PIR table; private notifications tell a multi-log subscriber which logs have news. 3-server cluster: 9,433 messages/s for 32,000 active users at 1.7 s end-to-end latency.
bitmessage_link: Pub/sub-shaped alternative to the flooded pool: a log secret (like a Bitmessage chan passphrase) fixes the read schedule, and PIR hides which log is read.

title: DP5: A Private Presence Service
note: Private presence and status updates: clients register presence and query friends' presence without revealing their buddy list, using epoch databases and PIR. A subscription service can support about 1 million users at roughly $0.50 per user per month; one evaluated configuration used about 15 core-minutes and 1 GB of bandwidth per epoch.
bitmessage_link: Private rendezvous that tells a contact it can reach you without a global address book; same job as Bitmessage's address publication but hiding the friend list.

title: MP3: A More Efficient Private Presence Protocol
note: Smaller presence database than DP5: about two-thirds of DP5's bandwidth at 200,000 users and about one-half at 1,000,000 users (savings grow with N), with client-facing latency about an order of magnitude lower.
bitmessage_link: Cuts the bandwidth of private rendezvous lookups, relevant to cost of any contact-aware recipient discovery.

title: PIR-PSI: Scaling Private Contact Discovery
note: Unbalanced PSI for a small client set against a huge user database, built from PIR and PSI techniques: a client with 1,024 contacts against 67 million users takes 1.36 s (multithreaded server) and 4.28 MiB of communication.
bitmessage_link: Bitmessage avoids contact discovery by publishing everything, but any scheme that routes by address or tag must solve how a user learns the right address or slot without revealing their contacts.

title: Mobile Private Contact Discovery at Scale
note: Improves two PSI protocols of Kiss et al. for mobile contact discovery, now secure against malicious clients: 2x less online communication for correlated OT, about 70% Cuckoo filter compression, 4.3x smaller filter updates, 8.2x less communication via LowMC instead of AES in the garbled-circuit PRF, 1,000x faster than prior smartphone implementations; integrated into Signal's client as proof of concept.
bitmessage_link: Bitmessage avoids contact discovery by publishing everything, but any scheme that routes by address or tag must solve how a user learns the right address or slot without revealing their contacts.

title: Scaling Mobile Private Contact Discovery to Billions of Users
note: Combines Kales et al. unbalanced PSI with the Kogan–Corrigan-Gibbs PIR; sublinear communication and online time; under 2 s on phones to query up to 1,024 contacts against a database of over 2 billion entries; setup communication up to 32x lower than prior mobile private contact discovery.
bitmessage_link: Bitmessage avoids contact discovery by publishing everything, but any scheme that routes by address or tag must solve how a user learns the right address or slot without revealing their contacts.

title: All the Numbers are US: Large-scale Abuse of Contact Discovery in Mobile Messengers
note: Crawling attacks on deployed contact discovery: with a database of mobile prefixes and few resources the authors queried 10% of US mobile numbers on WhatsApp and 100% on Signal; Telegram's API exposes sensitive data even for unregistered numbers; hash-based discovery is broken by efficient hash reversal; proposes incremental discovery.
bitmessage_link: Shows that address-lookup and enumeration is itself a metadata leak; Bitmessage avoids it only by not having a directory.

title: Contact Discovery in Mobile Messengers: Low-cost Attacks, Quantitative Analyses, and Efficient Mitigations
note: Extended journal version of the NDSS 2021 study: larger cross-messenger measurement, quantitative analysis of abuse and rate-limiting mitigations for WhatsApp, Signal and Telegram.
bitmessage_link: Bitmessage avoids contact discovery by publishing everything, but any scheme that routes by address or tag must solve how a user learns the right address or slot without revealing their contacts.

title: Distributed PIR: Scaling Private Messaging via the Users' Machines
note: DPIR: the message server delegates PIR work to clients in proportion to the messages each client reads and verifies delegates' results, evicting cheaters; asymptotically better scalability than prior PIR messaging with the same threat model, and 3.25x and 4.31x faster than two prior systems in the prototype, with the gap growing with the user base.
bitmessage_link: Makes PIR-based mailbox retrieval scale by having the readers share the work, the PIR analogue of every Bitmessage node carrying the load of the flood.

title: Pantheon: Private Retrieval from Public Key-Value Store
note: Single-round private lookup in a public key-value store, 93x lower server-side latency than the prior state of the art through refined cryptography and massive parallelism; no numbers recorded beyond that.
bitmessage_link: Key-value lookup by tag is the retrieval primitive for a topic-addressed Bitmessage replacement.

title: LetoPIR: Fast Keyword Private Information Retrieval with Logarithmic Communication
note: Hintless keyword PIR with logarithmic communication: 12.4x-17.0x less communication than SparsePIR (USENIX'23) for databases of 256 MB to 4 GB with 256-byte records and over 3x less computation at 256 MB; 51.4x-184.8x less communication than KPIR (USENIX'25) at similar or better computation. Notes that Apple already deploys PIR for real-time caller ID lookup.
bitmessage_link: Lowest-communication keyword lookup so far, directly usable for topic or tag retrieval.

title: PIR with Client-Side Preprocessing: Information-Theoretic Constructions and Lower Bounds
note: First study of information-theoretic single-server PIR with client preprocessing: new constructions with trade-offs between server computation, client space and bandwidth, a near-tight client-space versus bandwidth lower bound, and a result that beating it with a natural syntactic computational scheme would imply a hard problem in SZK.
bitmessage_link: Mailbox/board systems that replace Bitmessage's flood with indexed or oblivious retrieval; they hide the recipient from the storage nodes but need a rendezvous or shared-secret schedule that Bitmessage addresses do not give.

title: IBE and PIR from Isogenies
note: First isogeny-based identity-based encryption (with anonymity: ciphertexts hide the recipient identity) and first isogeny-based single-server PIR with polylogarithmic communication; plausibly post-quantum. Theory result, no concrete costs.
bitmessage_link: A route to identity-addressed, recipient-hiding encryption (the Bitmessage address model) with post-quantum security.

title: Unobservable Communication over Fully Untrusted Infrastructure
note: Pung: messaging as a PIR-backed key-value store where labels derive from shared secrets and a PRF, so servers never learn who talks to whom; private multi-retrieval, power-of-two-choices and batch codes make PIR practical, handling about 10^3 times more users than prior systems with a similar threat model. End-to-end latency up to 1.3 s with 1 million stored tuples on an under-utilised cluster; 36.2 s to retrieve 128 messages at 1M tuples.
bitmessage_link: Closest PIR-based replacement for Bitmessage's pool: recipient fetches its labelled slots by CPIR rather than trial-decrypting everything; needs a pre-shared secret to compute labels.

title: Riposte: An Anonymous Messaging System Handling Millions of Users
note: Anonymous broadcast to a shared bulletin board by writing into a database with a distributed point function (the PIR dual), DC-net-style traffic-analysis resistance, and client-proof DoS prevention; three non-colluding servers build an anonymity set of 2,895,216 users in 32 hours for latency-tolerant workloads. Recipients read the whole board.
bitmessage_link: Private-write counterpart to PIR read: hides the sender while the board is read in full, as in Bitmessage; shows write cost per message grows with board size.

title: Express: Lowering the Cost of Metadata-hiding Communication with Cryptographic Privacy
note: Two-server mailbox system using distributed point functions: constant-factor overhead per message independent of user count (Pung and Riposte grow roughly with sqrt of users), symmetric crypto only, over 100x less bandwidth than Pung and Riposte and 6x lower end-to-end cost of a whistleblowing application.
bitmessage_link: Per-recipient mailboxes written privately via DPF and read by identifier: removes the shared flood, but trusts that the two servers do not collude.

title: Alpenhorn: Bootstrapping Secure Communication without Leaking Metadata
note: Private first-contact: friend requests encrypted with anytrust IBE to an email-address identity, mailbox buckets, Bloom-filter dial tokens and keywheels evolving pairwise secrets for forward secrecy. 10 million users on three servers: average dial latency 150 s and client bandwidth overhead 3.7 KB/s; clients trial-detect within a bucket.
bitmessage_link: Solves how two parties learn each other's key and rendezvous without a directory leak, where Bitmessage looks up public keys on the network.

title: Addra: Metadata-private voice communication over fully untrusted infrastructure
note: FHE-PIR mailboxes for real-time voice: with 80 server machines, 32K clients at 99th-percentile message latency of 726 ms (Pung: 5.2 s), per-client 1.46 Mbps down and 30 Kbps up; PIR cost grows quadratically in users, so it does not reach hundreds of thousands.
bitmessage_link: Shows the latency and scale ceiling of PIR mailboxes (quadratic in users) that a flood-free Bitmessage successor would hit.

title: Fuzzy Message Detection (Penumbra protocol specification)
venue: Penumbra protocol docs (spec); design issue opened 2021-07-08
note: Deployed-chain specification of FMD: receiver FMD (receiver picks false-positive rate) and sender FMD (S-FMD: sender picks a consensus-determined rate, so precision adapts to global message rate), construction with constant-size keys, dummy clues so every transaction has as many clues as outputs, threat model, and a parameter-considerations page on statistical attacks that exploit knowledge of total messages and true positives. Page text saved, six sub-pages concatenated; undated, authorship by Penumbra Labs (design issue by hdevalence).
bitmessage_link: Production adaptation of Beck et al.'s FMD for a shielded chain; the fix for scanning that Bitmessage lacks, with explicit leakage when the false-positive rate is wrong.

title: ZIP 307: Light Client Protocol for Payment Detection
note: Light-client scheme for Sapling: a proxy serves compact blocks so wallets trial-decrypt locally and the proxy cannot tell which outputs are theirs. Full Sapling output ciphertext is 580 bytes plus 32-byte ephemeral key; the compact output keeps 116 bytes (ephemeral key, note commitment, first 52 ciphertext bytes), an 80% bandwidth cut, and a compact spend is 32 bytes (90% cut). Detection cost is a trial decryption per output on the client.
bitmessage_link: Exactly Bitmessage's recipient model on a chain: every client downloads and trial-decrypts everything, with bandwidth trimmed by dropping the memo.

title: Zcash Protocol Specification (Sapling and Orchard note encryption and viewing keys)
venue: Zcash protocol specification (living document; version v2026.7.0-236 NU6.2, 2026-09-30 downloaded)
note: Normative definition of note encryption: a wallet decrypts every output using its incoming viewing key (section 4.20.2 'Decryption using an Incoming Viewing Key'), with ECDH key agreement, a KDF and ChaCha20-Poly1305 per output; diversified addresses let one key serve many unlinkable addresses; no outsourced detection primitive in the base protocol.
bitmessage_link: Concrete deployed analogue of the problem: the per-output scan cost and the bandwidth/privacy compromise made by wallets that cannot afford to download and trial-decrypt everything.

title: BIP 352: Silent Payments
note: Static payment addresses with no on-chain notification: sender derives a unique taproot output from the sum of its input keys and the recipient's scan and spend keys, so the receiver does one ECDH per eligible transaction (summed input key) instead of per input. Scan-DoS is bounded by capping recipients sharing one scan key at K_max = 2323 per block. Light-client appendix: an index server serves 33 bytes of tweak data per eligible transaction, about 450 MB/month worst case (3500 eligible txs/block), 7-12 kB per block (30-50 MB/month) at observed 2023-2024 taproot usage, and about 30 MB/month if the client scans once every 3 days using cut-through; outputs are then matched with BIP 158 filters.
bitmessage_link: Concrete deployed analogue of the problem: the per-output scan cost and the bandwidth/privacy compromise made by wallets that cannot afford to download and trial-decrypt everything.

title: BIP 47: Reusable Payment Codes for Hierarchical Deterministic Wallets
note: Public payment code from which sender and receiver derive per-payment addresses after an on-chain notification transaction; the receiver finds notifications by watching its notification address, so scanning is cheap but the notification link is public.
bitmessage_link: Trades the stealth scan for a public notification, the opposite of Bitmessage's fully ambiguous broadcast.

title: BIP 158: Compact Block Filters for Light Clients (with BIP 157)
note: Server publishes one Golomb-coded-set filter per block; the client downloads filters and matches its own scripts locally, fetching blocks on a hit, so the server learns nothing from the filter requests (unlike BIP 37). Costs: a filter download per block for every client, trading bandwidth for privacy. Page text of BIP 158 saved; BIP 157 text saved at 2017-bip157-clientfilters.md.
bitmessage_link: Client-side filtering is the middle point between full download and PIR: a per-block digest the client tests locally, as Bitmessage's tag-prefix streams could be.

title: BIP 157: Client Side Block Filtering
note: P2P messages and commitments (filter headers) for fetching compact block filters; companion to BIP 158.
bitmessage_link: Protocol half of the client-side filtering design.

title: BIP 37: Connection Bloom Filtering
note: SPV client sends a Bloom filter to a full node, which forwards only matching transactions; false-positive rate is the client's privacy knob. Attacked by Gervais et al. (ACSAC 2014): under 20 addresses leaks almost all of them.
bitmessage_link: Bloom-filter subscription to a relay, the deployed form of tag filtering, with documented leakage.

title: ERC-5564: Stealth Addresses
note: Announcer contract publishes ephemeral key plus metadata whose first byte is a view tag (first byte of the hash of the shared secret). Per announcement a recipient computes one ECDH multiplication and one hash and compares the tag; on mismatch it skips the second multiplication and address derivation. The tag reveals 8 bits of the shared-secret hash and gives 1/256 false matches.
bitmessage_link: Cheap 1-byte tag that lets the recipient discard 255/256 of announcements, a minimal fuzzy detection that leaks 8 bits to the announcer's observers.

title: ERC-6538: Stealth Meta-Address Registry
note: Canonical on-chain registry mapping a registrant to its stealth meta-address, so a sender can find the recipient's scan and spend keys without interaction.
bitmessage_link: A public key directory for stealth keys; the discovery step that Bitmessage does with address-to-pubkey requests.

title: Reduce scan times with 1-byte-per-output 'view tag' (Monero Research Lab issue 73)
note: Proposal to add a 1-byte view tag per output (first byte of a hash of the sender-receiver shared secret) so the wallet skips the remaining elliptic-curve operations for about 255/256 of outputs; proposer estimates a 50-70% scan reduction.
bitmessage_link: Same 8-bit fuzzy pre-filter as ERC-5564, in a chain where every wallet scans every output.

title: Add view tags to outputs to reduce wallet scanning time (monero PR 8061)
note: Implementation of view tags: measured scanning-time reductions of 30-40% or more on the author's machine; about 99.6% of outputs skip the expensive elliptic-curve step; an optional faster hash gave a further 1.5%.
bitmessage_link: Measured payoff of an 8-bit pre-filter in a deployed wallet.

title: EIP-627: Whisper Specification
note: Whisper envelopes carry a 4-byte topic; peers exchange a 512-bit Bloom filter (up to three bits per topic) so neighbours forward only messages whose topics match, with PoW on envelopes. The filter is a deliberate privacy-versus-bandwidth knob. Direct Ethereum-side cousin of Bitmessage.
bitmessage_link: Whisper is the closest deployed sibling of Bitmessage: PoW envelopes, flooding, and Bloom-filter topic interest to cut bandwidth.

title: 2PPS: Publish/Subscribe with Provable Privacy
note: Pub/sub with provable privacy for both sides: publishers write via distributed-point-function secret sharing, subscribers read topics via PIR, security holds while one server is honest. Prototype: 100,000 concurrent active clients with 5 s end-to-end latency and lower bandwidth than comparable systems.
bitmessage_link: Topic-based publish/subscribe where the subscriber's topic is hidden from the servers by PIR, instead of Bitmessage's every-node-sees-everything flood.

title: Private Set Intersection for Unequal Set Sizes with Mobile Applications
note: Turns four PSI protocols into precomputation form so setup communication is linear in the large set and online communication linear in the small set; compares them on PC and smartphone: garbled-AES wins setup and PC online time, Diffie-Hellman wins mobile online time.
bitmessage_link: Bitmessage avoids contact discovery by publishing everything, but any scheme that routes by address or tag must solve how a user learns the right address or slot without revealing their contacts.

title: Fast Private Set Intersection from Homomorphic Encryption
note: FHE-based PSI with communication O(Ny log Nx) for set sizes Ny < Nx: intersecting five thousand 32-bit strings with 16 million takes 36 s online, 71 s of receiver-independent preprocessing and 12.5 MB round-trip, a 38-115x communication reduction over prior work.
bitmessage_link: Bitmessage avoids contact discovery by publishing everything, but any scheme that routes by address or tag must solve how a user learns the right address or slot without revealing their contacts.

title: SoK: Outsourced Private Set Intersection
note: Framework of 12 properties (security, functionality, efficiency) and analysis of 20 outsourced PSI protocols where clients delegate the heavy work to an untrusted server, with an interactive selection tool and gaps relative to ordinary PSI.
bitmessage_link: Bitmessage avoids contact discovery by publishing everything, but any scheme that routes by address or tag must solve how a user learns the right address or slot without revealing their contacts.

title: Fast Proxy Re-Encryption for Publish/Subscribe Systems
note: Two multi-hop unidirectional lattice PRE schemes (NTRU-ABD-PRE, BV-PRE) so a publisher encrypts without knowing the subscriber and a server delegates access; BV-PRE has lower time and space than prior IND-CPA lattice PRE. Confidentiality delegation rather than recipient hiding.
bitmessage_link: none direct; shows how a pub/sub server can route confidential data to subscribers whom the publisher does not know.

title: Anonymity of NIST PQC Round 3 KEMs
note: Proves anonymity (and, with a suitable DEM, robustness) of the hybrid PKEs from NTRU, BIKE, FrodoKEM, HQC (except two of three parameter sets), NTRU LPRime and SIKE in the QROM, and anonymity of Classic McEliece; notes technical gaps in Kyber, Saber and Streamlined NTRU Prime IND-CCA proofs. Answers the open question of Grubbs, Maram and Paterson.
bitmessage_link: Says which post-quantum KEM choices keep ciphertexts recipient-anonymous, required if Bitmessage-style flooding is to survive a PQ migration.

title: Privacy-Preserving Data Publish-Subscribe Service on Cloud-based Platforms
note: Bi-policy ABE lets the encryptor set an access policy and the decryptor a filtering policy, so an untrusted cloud server evaluates both without learning subscriptions or data (PDPS); secure in the standard model, with performance evaluation in the paper.
bitmessage_link: Server-side matching of encrypted data to encrypted subscriptions, the pub/sub form of outsourced detection.

title: A Lattice-based Publish-Subscribe Communication Protocol using Accelerated Homomorphic Encryption Primitives
note: GPU acceleration of lattice KP-ABE encryption and homomorphic evaluation for pub/sub: 2.1x (encrypt) and 13.2x (homomorphic evaluation) faster than CPU on an i9, supporting up to 128 attributes.
bitmessage_link: Cost data for attribute-policy matching on encrypted pub/sub messages.

title: A Note on Notes: Towards Scalable Anonymous Payments via Evolving Nullifiers and Oblivious Synchronization
note: Oblivious synchronization: a user asks an untrusted remote service that ingests the public ledger for succinct proofs that its coins are unspent and valid; the service is oblivious to the client's transactions, keeps only ephemeral per-client state, and clients can switch services. Primarily about pruning the ever-growing nullifier set, not note discovery; included as the Zcash designers' model for outsourcing wallet work to untrusted servers.
bitmessage_link: Same delegation idea (an untrusted server does the heavy per-ledger work for a client without learning its transactions) applied to coin-state proofs instead of message detection.

title: ZLiTE: Lightweight Clients for Shielded Zcash Transactions using Trusted Execution
note: States the problem plainly: to receive a Zerocash payment the recipient must scan the whole chain testing each transaction, impractical on mobile. ZLiTE lets a server with a TEE do the scan for a light client, with side-channel-hardened processing and a bandwidth-efficient way to keep spend witnesses fresh. Trust shifts to the TEE vendor; no number recorded here.
bitmessage_link: TEE-assisted outsourcing of exactly Bitmessage's trial decryption, the same trust assumption that private signaling with SGX makes.

title: Privacy Comparison for Bitcoin Light Client Implementations
note: Defines privacy metrics and compares SPV (BIP 37 Bloom filters) with Neutrino (BIP 157/158 filters) on real Bitcoin data over time, showing the privacy-versus-communication trade-off; proposes general privacy-enhancing techniques and an SPV 'aggregation model' with better privacy.
bitmessage_link: Measured privacy/bandwidth trade-off of the two deployed ways to avoid downloading everything: server-side Bloom filter versus client-side filtering.

title: OCash: Fully Anonymous Payments between Blockchain Light Clients
note: Anonymous payments where the light client stays private even from the full nodes it reads through: a tree-ORAM variant shuffles payments on-chain while telling the client a few positions among which to find its payment, so it never scans the chain nor reveals which entries it reads. UC-proved; introduces anonymous-coin-friendly encryption and compressible randomness beacons. No concrete cost figure recorded here.
bitmessage_link: Position-hint approach to finding your messages: the recipient fetches a few candidate slots instead of trial-decrypting everything, with the slot choice hidden from the serving node.

title: XPIR: Private Information Retrieval for Everyone
note: Shows with lattice-based (ring-LWE) homomorphic encryption that single-database computational PIR is practical, overturning the 2007 Sion-Carbunar conclusion that cPIR would never beat downloading the whole database; free GPLv3 implementation. Baseline PIR library later improved by SealPIR. No single headline figure recorded here.
bitmessage_link: Turning point for the argument 'just download everything': after XPIR a per-recipient retrieval can cost less than the full flood on a fast network.

title: Private Information Retrieval with Sublinear Online Time
note: First PIR with sublinear online server time and no extra server storage, through an offline phase where the client fetches a short hint before choosing its index: statistical security with two servers, computational with one; proven optimal for the communication versus time trade-off in this model. Origin of the client-preprocessing line (Piano, TreePIR, Plinko).
bitmessage_link: Replaces broadcast-and-trial-decrypt with indexed private retrieval: the recipient fetches only its slots and the server learns nothing about which; works only if the recipient can compute or look up the slot, which Bitmessage's address-less flooding does not provide.

title: Private Blocklist Lookups with Checklist
note: Two-server PIR system with sublinear server time, applied to Google Safe Browsing lookups in Firefox: 3.3x more communication and 9.8x more server compute than the leaky partial-hash lookups, but 6.7x lower end-to-end server cost than prior two-server PIR. Its PIR is reused in the private contact discovery of Hetz et al.
bitmessage_link: Concrete price of making a high-volume membership lookup private instead of broadcasting a list, the comparison point for any hash-prefix or tag lookup.

title: Single-Server Private Information Retrieval with Sublinear Amortized Time
note: First single-server PIR with sublinear amortized server time, sublinear extra storage and adaptive queries from standard assumptions (DDH, QR, LWE): the client downloads a hint costing linear server time once, then a bounded number of queries are answered in sublinear time; lower bound shows the best scheme is optimal for server online time versus client storage.
bitmessage_link: Replaces broadcast-and-trial-decrypt with indexed private retrieval: the recipient fetches only its slots and the server learns nothing about which; works only if the recipient can compute or look up the slot, which Bitmessage's address-less flooding does not provide.
